c1:p0: This opening sentence introduces Vernon's Bank, a prestigious financial institution in the Home Counties that was considered nearly as stable and secure as the Bank of England itself. It establishes the bank's reputation and importance as the foundation for understanding the subsequent narrative about the Vernon family and the bank's eventual crisis.
c1:p1: This chunk contrasts the sophisticated financial community's measured view of Vernon's Bank with the unquestioning faith of its ordinary rural clients—shopkeepers, farmers, and laborers—who regarded it as absolutely secure and stable, setting up the dramatic irony of their later panic when rumors of the bank's failure emerge.
c1:p2: This chunk appears in the opening section of the chapter and establishes the historical foundation and reputation of Vernon's Bank. It follows the introduction of the bank's status among educated classes and precedes the explanation of John Vernon's exceptional business acumen. The passage introduces the "golden touch" quality that made the bank legendary and secure in the eyes of common people throughout the region.
c1:p3: This chunk reflects on the mysterious quality that made John Vernon, the bank's founder, extraordinarily successful in financial matters. It compares his inexplicable talent for making money grow to artistic genius, as the narrator struggles to explain why he succeeded where other equally diligent men failed.
c1:p4: This passage describes John Vernon, the grandfather of the current bank head, explaining the special gift or genius he possessed that made him exceptionally successful in banking and investments, far surpassing other capable men in the field. It illustrates why Vernon's Bank became known as second only to the Bank of England in stability and strength.
c1:p5: This chunk describes a critical moment in the career of John Vernon, the grandfather of the current bank head, demonstrating his exceptional financial genius. During a financial panic and bank run that would have destroyed any ordinary banker, John Vernon alone managed to survive and emerge even stronger, establishing the foundation for Vernon's Bank's legendary reputation for stability and invulnerability.
c1:p6: This chunk discusses John Vernon (the grandfather), the founding figure of Vernon's Bank, and his remarkable financial success during a banking panic. It explains how he mysteriously survived a run on the bank that would have ruined other bankers, and then contrasts his exceptional money-making ability with his son Edward's more modest but still competent financial management of the established family fortune.
c1:p7: This chunk describes the family misfortunes of Edward Vernon, the son of the wealthy banker John Vernon (the grandfather). It explains how Edward had two sons—one died young leaving a daughter to be raised by her grandfather, and the other son went wrong morally and also died, leaving behind a helpless family. This family tragedy sets up the backstory for the current generation of Vernons and foreshadows the problems that will plague the banking house through poor decisions and moral failings.
c1:p8: This chunk appears in paragraph P8 and describes the tragic family history of the Vernon banking house. It explains how John Vernon (the current head of the bank) is the son of Edward Vernon's younger son, who "went wrong" and died, leaving young John to be raised by his widowed mother with hopes he would marry his cousin Catherine Vernon to reunite the family fortune.
c1:p9: This chunk introduces the current John Vernon, the protagonist's cousin, who initially showed promise as a capable banker resembling his great-grandfather. It marks the turning point where, upon inheriting leadership of Vernon's Bank after the death of the senior partner, he begins to display troubling behavioral changes that will ultimately lead to the bank's financial ruin.
c1:p10: This chunk describes the failed engagement between John Vernon and his cousin Catherine Vernon. After the grandfather's death, their planned marriage is abruptly called off without explanation from either party. John dismisses questions about the broken engagement with evasive laughter, while Catherine maintains dignified silence. This romantic disappointment sets up the family conflict and Catherine's later role as a neglected partner in the banking business.
c1:p11: John Vernon's mother intervenes in the broken engagement between her son and his cousin Catherine Vernon, attempting to convince them to marry so that Catherine's money remains in the family business. c1:p12: The chunk occurs in the context of the failed engagement between John Vernon and his cousin Catherine Vernon. His mother actively intervenes, attempting to persuade both of them to proceed with the marriage by emphasizing the financial advantages of keeping Catherine's money within the Vernon family business. Catherine responds with dignified silence, while John dismisses his mother's concerns about the bank's stability depending on retaining her wealth.
c1:p13: John Vernon dismisses his mother's concerns about his marriage to Catherine falling through and his excessive spending. He scoffs at her understanding of the banking business, rejecting her warnings that his extravagant lifestyle and the loss of Catherine's money to the firm could damage Vernon's Bank. His mother's pleas go unheeded as the younger generation asserts its independence.
c1:p14: This passage describes Mrs. Vernon's futile attempts to remonstrate with her son John about his extravagant spending and neglect of his duties as head of the bank, particularly regarding his broken engagement to his cousin Catherine. c15:p32: Edward encounters Hester on her return from Redborough and, after commenting on her proud bearing, suddenly accuses her of intending to marry Harry. c15:p35: Edward Vernon confronts Hester on the road, calmly analyzing her situation and suggesting that she should marry Harry for financial security and social position, since marriage is her only path to power and independence as a woman.
c15:p36: Edward Vernon encounters Hester on her return from Redborough and manipulates her with calm, reasoned arguments about her necessity to marry Harry for financial security and social advancement. c15:p40: Hester encounters Edward Vernon on the Common as she returns from her errand in Redborough. c15:p42: Edward Vernon confronts Hester on the Common and attempts to justify his insulting behavior toward her by arguing that without protection or consequences, men naturally treat unprotected women badly. He claims this is simply human nature, no worse than his neighbors.

c15:p45: Edward Vernon encounters Hester on her return from Redborough and, after initially flattering her perceptiveness, begins making increasingly inappropriate and threatening remarks. c21:p110: Captain Morgan reflects on mortality while watching Roland depart. He observes that he and his wife have outlived Roland's parents despite being older, and expresses existential concern about their continued survival and their responsibility to Catherine Vernon's household.

c22:p0: This chunk opens the chapter and introduces Ellen Merridew's initiative to establish herself as a social leader in Redborough through hosting weekly dances (Thés Dansantes). It marks the beginning of Ellen's plan to invite Hester to assist her, which will launch Hester into social society and set in motion the emotional entanglements with Edward and Harry that dominate the remainder of the chapter.
c22:p1: Ellen Merridew, newly married and returned to Redborough, asserts her newfound independence and social authority as a married woman, contrasting her current position with her previous status as a young unmarried woman under her aunt's oversight. Despite her self-centered nature, she is motivated to take up Hester's cause partly by her own ambitions to host fashionable social gatherings.
c22:p2: This passage describes Ellen Merridew's character - her willingness to help others is conditional and self-serving, motivated by her own interests rather than genuine benevolence. It establishes her as a woman of shallow virtue who helps others only when it benefits her, setting up her later offer to help Hester with social gatherings, which is ultimately driven by Ellen's need for assistance with her own social events rather than kindness toward her cousin.
c22:p3: Ellen Merridew visits the Vernonry to recruit Hester as her assistant for her weekly social gatherings called "Thés Dansantes." While Harry and Algernon had previously suggested Ellen help brighten Hester's life, Ellen's primary motivation is practical: she needs Hester's help to ensure her Thursday parties are successful, as she refuses to rely on the Merridew sisters-in-law, whom she considers inferior to herself despite her marriage into their family.
c22:p4: Ellen Merridew, newly returned to Redborough as a married woman, decides to establish herself socially by hosting weekly Thursday gatherings called "Thés Dansantes." Recognizing she needs assistance to make these events successful, she sets out in her fashionable carriage to visit the Vernonry to recruit Hester Vernon as her assistant, viewing her young cousin as the perfect helper to manage her social ambitions.
c22:p5: Ellen Merridew arrives at the Vernonry in her fashionable carriage to visit Hester and her mother, Mrs. John. She is dressed elaborately in new sealskin furs and jewelry, presenting an impressive appearance as she prepares to propose that Hester help her organize fashionable Thursday evening dances (Thés Dansantes) in her new household.
c22:p6: Ellen Merridew arrives at the Vernonry in her new carriage, dressed in fashionable sealskin and finery, to visit Hester and propose that she become her assistant at the social gatherings Ellen plans to host. c22:p7: Ellen arrives at the Vernonry in her new carriage and fashionable attire to propose that Hester help her organize social gatherings called "Thés Dansantes." The Vernon-Ridgway sisters, observing from their windows, make dismissive comments about Ellen's display of wealth and finery.
c22:p8: Ellen Merridew arrives at the Vernonry in an impressive carriage and fur coat to visit Mrs. John and Hester. c22:p9: Ellen Merridew arrives at the Vernonry in her impressive carriage to visit Hester and her mother Mrs. John, but the other residents—the Miss Vernon-Ridgways sisters and Mr. Mildmay Vernon—observe her arrival from behind curtains and windows, surprised and skeptical about her unexpected visit to see Mrs. John rather than themselves.
c22:p10: Ellen Merridew arrives at the Vernonry in an impressive carriage and expensive furs. The Vernon-Ridgway sisters watch from behind curtains, initially assuming Ellen has come to visit them. c22:p11: Ellen arrives at the Vernonry in her new victoria to visit Hester and propose that Hester help her organize social gatherings called Thés Dansantes. c22:p12: Ellen Merridew arrives at the Vernonry in her fashionable victoria to visit Mrs. John and Hester. c22:p13: Ellen arrives at the Vernonry in her new carriage and expensive furs to propose that Hester become her assistant for organizing social gatherings called Thés Dansantes. c22:p14: Ellen Merridew arrives unexpectedly at the Vernonry to visit Hester and her mother, Mrs. John, in her fashionable new carriage. c22:p15: Ellen Merridew arrives at the Vernonry in her carriage to visit Hester and her mother, Mrs. John. c22:p16: Ellen Merridew visits Hester and her mother at the Vernonry to propose that Hester become her assistant at the social gatherings she plans to host. c22:p17: Ellen Merridew visits the Vernonry to propose that Hester help her organize weekly "Thés Dansantes" (tea dances), framing it as an opportunity for Hester to meet eligible society members. c22:p18: Ellen Merridew has visited the Vernonry to propose that Hester help her organize weekly social dances (Thés Dansantes). c22:p19: Ellen Merridew visits the Vernonry to propose that Hester help her organize weekly "Thés Dansantes" (tea dances). c22:p20: Mrs. John reflects on her reduced circumstances and expresses regret that her daughter Hester cannot enjoy the social advantages she herself had in youth. c22:p21: Mrs. John expresses her willingness to allow Hester to participate in Ellen's social gatherings, acknowledging her regret that her daughter has needed help from a relation but ultimately consenting to the arrangement for Hester's social advancement.
c22:p22: Ellen visits the Vernonry to propose that Hester help her organize weekly social gatherings called "Thés Dansantes." Mrs. John eagerly accepts the proposal, seeing it as an excellent opportunity for her daughter. Ellen, dressed in fashionable new sealskin furs and accessories, throws off her coat while discussing the arrangement with Mrs. John, who admires the rare garment.
c22:p23: Ellen Merridew arrives at the Vernonry in her fashionable carriage, wearing luxurious furs and accessories, to recruit Hester as her assistant for her social gatherings. Mrs. John, Hester's mother, observes Ellen's wealth and elegance with a mixture of admiration and nostalgia, remembering her own prosperous past before her husband's death, and hoping her daughter will achieve similar social and material success through marriage.
c22:p24: Mrs. John observes Ellen's elegant appearance—her sealskin coat, victoria carriage, and fashionable accessories—and reflects wistfully on her own lost youth and former prosperity, wishing her daughter Hester could achieve the same social advantages and material success through advantageous marriage.
c22:p25: Ellen Merridew visits Hester at the Vernonry to propose that Hester become her assistant for her new weekly dancing parties (Thés Dansantes). Despite Hester's initial prideful rejection of what she sees as charity, she is secretly excited by the prospect of attending regular dances in society, a rare opportunity in Redborough.

c24:p90: Emma eagerly insists on accompanying Hester to Redborough, expressing her desire to see the town and meet the local people, as she is uncertain how long her visit will last. She finishes her knitting heel before preparing to leave with Hester, demonstrating her characteristic practical attention to detail while pursuing her social ambitions in this new place.
c24:p91: Emma encounters Hester on her way to Redborough and insists on accompanying her, eager to explore the town and meet local people while discussing her situation as a dependent living with her brother Roland.
c24:p92: Emma has just asked to accompany Hester to Redborough for a shopping trip. Mrs. Morgan expresses concern about whether Hester minds, as Emma goes upstairs to fetch her hat. Hester's mixed feelings are revealed—she is not particularly enthusiastic about Emma as a person, but is drawn to the novelty of having a new companion to take into town.
c24:p93: Hester is leaving with Emma to go to Redborough and asks Mrs. Morgan a question about Catherine Vernon before Emma returns downstairs, but hesitates to ask it fully, saying she cannot speak before someone else.
c24:p94: Hester hesitates to ask Mrs. Morgan a question about Catherine Vernon before Emma returns from upstairs, saying she heard something concerning about Catherine the night before.
c24:p95: Hester is preparing to go into Redborough with Emma Ashton when Mrs. Morgan asks her a question about Catherine Vernon. Hester begins to answer but stops herself, saying she cannot speak about it in front of Emma, and then agrees she is ready to leave.
c24:p96: Emma Ashton is being introduced to the household and is accompanying Hester to Redborough. As they walk together, Emma explains her family background and her dependent situation, revealing that she comes from a large, poor family of eight children and was raised by her eldest sister Elinor after their father's death. She emphasizes her need to marry for security and her desire to be called by her first name rather than the formal "Miss Ashton," which reminds her of her near-governess status.
c24:p97: Emma explains to Hester how her married siblings have failed to provide her adequate support and housing, each trying to minimize their responsibility for her care while she was passed between their households.
c24:p98: Emma explains to Hester how she managed her living arrangements among her sisters' households, refusing to allow one sister to shirk her turn in hosting her while protecting another sister from being overburdened, thereby narrowly avoiding becoming a governess.
c24:p99: Emma discusses her family situation and dependence on her brother Roland, explaining how she avoided becoming a governess despite nearly being forced into that position. Hester responds by suggesting that independence as a governess would have been preferable to Emma's current state of dependence.
c24:p100: Emma justifies her decision to remain financially dependent on her brother Roland rather than become a governess, explaining that taking a paid position would harm her marriage prospects—her primary life goal—since all her sisters have married well.
c24:p101: Emma Ashton explains to Hester that she has deliberately avoided becoming a governess because it would damage her "chance" of marriage, which she views as an essential necessity for securing her future independence and comfort. When Hester questions what Emma means by her "chance," she responds with moral disapproval at Emma's frank admission that marriage is her primary objective, but Emma remains oblivious to any judgment, treating matrimony as a practical and unquestionable life goal rather than something worthy of shame or criticism.
c24:p102: Emma explains her desperate circumstances and pragmatic approach to marriage. Having been passed among her married sisters without a permanent home, she was nearly forced into governessing when her sister Bee refused to accommodate her during a visit. She defends her focus on finding a husband as a practical necessity for securing her own household and independence, dismissing any suggestion that such pragmatism is improper.
c24:p103: Emma recounts to Hester her family circumstances and explains how she came to live with her brother Roland. She describes how her sisters were unwilling to take her in—particularly Bee, who deliberately began renovations to avoid having Emma stay with her. Rather than become a governess, which would have damaged her marriage prospects, Emma accepted Roland's offer to live with him when he acquired his own house, a situation she views as preferable to her previous dependence on her various siblings.
c24:p104: Emma describes her living arrangement with her brother Roland to Hester, explaining how he took her in after she nearly became a governess, offering her a home with minimal duties and a clothing allowance in exchange for her companionship.
c24:p105: Emma Ashton describes her dependent situation living with her brother Roland without shame or resentment, viewing marriage as an elemental necessity and her unpaid domestic role as a practical arrangement. Hester reacts with shocked indignation to Emma's casual acceptance of dependency, revealing her own sensitive pride and contrasting values about independence and self-respect.
c24:p106: Hester reacts with moral shock to Emma's matter-of-fact account of her dependent situation among her various sisters' households, where she was passed around as an burden despite never complaining or demanding special treatment. Though Emma's pragmatic acceptance of this neglect disturbs Hester's sensibility, the narrator notes that Emma herself harbors no resentment toward her sisters for their callousness.
c24:p107: Emma defends her decision to live with her brother Roland rather than work as a governess, explaining that while being a governess would be more independent, it would damage her marriage prospects—her primary concern. She dismisses Hester's suggestion that governessing would be preferable, arguing that her dependent position with Roland, though duller, allows her to preserve her "chance" of making an advantageous match.
c24:p108: Emma is describing to Hester the relative advantages of living with her various married sisters compared to her current domestic situation with her brother Roland. She is explaining how, despite the lack of formal attention, staying with her sisters exposed her to social opportunities and people, which she values for improving her matrimonial prospects.
c24:p109: Emma is walking through Redborough with Hester, asking questions about the town and the people living there. She has just been describing her life with her sister Elinor and how it compares to her current situation with her brother Roland. Upon spotting a large red house near the road, she inquires about it, remarking that nice people ought to live there—unaware that this is Catherine Vernon's house, the Grange.
c24:p110: Emma Ashton, a newly arrived visitor, is walking through Redborough with Hester Vernon. As they pass a large red house near the road, Hester identifies it as Catherine Vernon's residence, blushing as she does so. Emma immediately expresses her intention to visit Catherine Vernon, despite Hester's reluctance and explanation that Catherine prefers to see the Vernons only under certain circumstances.
c24:p111: Emma, having just learned that the large red house nearby is Catherine Vernon's residence, eagerly expresses her intention to visit Catherine immediately, assuming she has free access as a family member.
c24:p112: Emma Ashton, newly arrived at her grandparents' house, eagerly seeks to visit Catherine Vernon at the Grange. When she spots the big red house near the road, she asks Hester to take her there at once. Hester responds with this statement, explaining that Catherine does not welcome visits from Hester and her family, only from Hester's grandparents, and that this cold treatment is deserved given the family tensions.
c24:p113: Emma Ashton, a young visitor seeking to make a good marriage, has just met Hester on the road to Redborough. As they walk together, Emma eagerly asks about Catherine Vernon's house and expresses her intention to visit. Edward Vernon emerges from Catherine's gate at this moment, creating tension between his obligation to Catherine and his encounter with Hester, whom he appears to have romantic feelings for.
c24:p114: Emma Ashton has just arrived in Redborough and is eager to meet the local society and find a husband. While walking with Hester toward town, they encounter Edward Vernon emerging from Catherine Vernon's gate. Emma, unaware of the family tensions and assuming Catherine lives alone, is intrigued by Edward's appearance and insists on being introduced to him, hoping he might help her secure an invitation to Mrs. Merridew's dancing party.
c24:p115: Emma Ashton, newly arrived at her grandfather's house, encounters Hester on the road to Redborough. When Edward Vernon hesitates at Catherine's gate—caught between avoiding Hester's disapproval and Catherine's scrutiny—he ultimately decides to approach them rather than retreat, prioritizing his need to escape Hester's disdain over Catherine's potential displeasure.
c24:p116: Edward encounters Hester and Emma on the road near Catherine Vernon's house. Despite his initial hesitation to meet them (aware of Catherine watching from inside), he decides that facing Hester's disdain is preferable to Catherine's disapproval, and steps forward to greet them cordially about the previous night's ball.
c24:p117: Emma Ashton, a distant cousin newly arrived at her grandfather's house, encounters Edward Vernon on the road while walking to Redborough with Hester. She eagerly requests an introduction to Edward and asks him to inform Catherine Vernon of her intention to visit, expressing surprise at the formal distance maintained between family members in this household.
c24:p118: Emma Ashton, a newly arrived cousin, is speaking to Edward Vernon about the formal and distant relationships among family members in Redborough. She contrasts this with her experience elsewhere, where relatives interact casually without reservation. Edward responds by acknowledging the family's coldness and lack of civility toward one another.
c24:p119: Emma Ashton, a newly arrived cousin seeking social advancement, encounters Edward Vernon on the road near Catherine Vernon's house while walking with Hester. Emma, unaware of family tensions, expresses surprise at the formality and distance between family members and asks Edward to help arrange an invitation to Mrs. Merridew's dancing party. Edward's response about the family's coldness toward one another characterizes the deep rifts dividing the Vernon cousins, particularly between Hester's branch and Catherine's.
c24:p120: Emma, a newly arrived cousin, encounters Edward Vernon on the road while walking with Hester toward Redborough. After Edward hesitantly greets them, Emma introduces herself and expresses her desire to visit Catherine Vernon and see the town. Edward laughs at the family's coldness toward each other. Emma then responds with feigned apology for detaining Hester, while characterizing herself as a stranger unfamiliar with the local family dynamics and asking Edward if he lives in the area before announcing that Hester will show her around Redborough.
c24:p121: Emma, a young cousin newly arrived in Redborough, is walking with Hester through town when they encounter Edward Vernon. Emma mentions wanting to see "the little town," and Edward corrects her, warning that the Redborough people would object to their town being called "little."
c24:p122: Emma Ashton, a newly arrived cousin, is walking with Hester toward Redborough town when they encounter Edward Vernon. Emma, eager to gain social acceptance and secure an invitation to Mrs. Merridew's dancing parties, asks Edward to help her obtain one and expresses interest in seeing the Bank that manages the Vernon family fortune.
c24:p123: Emma asks Edward Vernon if Mrs. Merridew, who hosts the dancing parties, is his sister, as she seeks to obtain an invitation to the social events in Redborough.
c24:p124: Emma Ashton, a new visitor to Redborough, encounters Edward Vernon on the road while walking with Hester. She asks him whether Mrs. Merridew, who hosts the dancing parties, is his sister, prompting his response that she is his cousin instead.
c24:p125: Emma Ashton encounters Edward Vernon on the road to Redborough while walking with Hester. She boldly requests his help in obtaining an invitation to Mrs. Merridew's dancing party, remarking on the family divisions that seem to prevent her from being invited through normal channels.
c24:p126: Emma Ashton, a young visitor to Redborough, encounters Edward Vernon on the road and directly asks him to help secure her an invitation to Mrs. Merridew's dancing party. She appeals to him by flattering gentlemen as more accommodating than ladies in such matters, and suggests he persuade Mrs. Merridew to send her a ticket despite the family tensions she claims not to understand.
c24:p127: Emma Ashton, a newly arrived cousin, is speaking to Edward Vernon on the road to Redborough. She is asking him to help her obtain an invitation to Mrs. Merridew's dancing parties and explaining her position as a neutral outsider in the family disputes that she has just learned about.
c24:p128: Edward Vernon agrees to help Emma Ashton obtain an invitation to Mrs. Merridew's dancing party and excuses himself to continue his work, while Hester deliberately slows her pace to avoid walking with him.
c24:p129: Emma, a newly arrived cousin staying with her grandparents, encounters Edward Vernon on the road while walking to Redborough with Hester. After Edward hesitantly approaches them and Emma boldly asks him to help secure her an invitation to Mrs. Merridew's dances, Edward attempts to excuse himself. Emma then questions whether they are all heading the same direction, prompting Hester to deliberately slow their pace to avoid walking together with Edward, which Emma interprets as evidence of a secret romance between them.
c24:p130: Emma Ashton, newly arrived at her grandfather's house, encounters Edward Vernon on the road while walking with Hester to Redborough. Emma, unaware of family tensions, persuades Edward to help her get an invitation to Mrs. Merridew's dancing party. As the three walk together, Hester becomes increasingly uncomfortable with Edward's presence near Catherine Vernon's house, and deliberately slows her pace to distance herself from him, while Edward hastens ahead, eager to escape the awkward situation.
c24:p131: Edward hastily departs from an encounter with Hester and the newly arrived Emma Ashton on the road near Catherine Vernon's house, walking at an unusually rapid pace. Hester deliberately slows her pace and points out local sights to Emma, creating an obvious contrast in their movements that leads Emma to suspect they are secret lovers kept apart by family conflict.
c24:p132: Emma Ashton, a visiting cousin, encounters Edward Vernon and Hester on the road near Catherine Vernon's house. After Edward hastily departs and Hester deliberately slows their pace to avoid walking with him, Emma observes their strange behavior and misinterprets it as evidence of a secret romance between them, unaware of the family tensions actually driving their apparent avoidance of each other.
c24:p133: Emma Ashton observes Edward Vernon and Hester walking separately on the road to Redborough, suspecting they are lovers kept apart by family conflict. She comments on the unnaturalness of such family divisions.
c24:p134: Emma Ashton criticizes the family divisions in Redborough, suggesting that Hester and Edward's reluctance to walk together openly due to family conflict is excessive, while she remains oblivious to the actual romantic tension between them.
c25:p0: Edward reflects on his uncharacteristic behavior at the Merridews' ball, where he openly admired Hester to Catherine, breaking from his usual cautious social restraint. This moment marks the beginning of his internal conflict between maintaining propriety and pursuing his growing attraction to Hester, which will lead him toward increasingly reckless financial speculation.
c25:p1: Edward has just made a bold statement to Hester about Catherine Vernon, abandoning his usual restraint. The chunk explains how the atmosphere of the Merridews' house—characterized by freedom and social liberty—has broken down his normally rigid adherence to propriety and social convention, both in formal settings like dances and in his professional life at the bank.
c25:p2: Edward's constrained social behavior at ordinary balls in Redborough, where he carefully manages his dance partners and social attentions according to propriety and the expectations of local families, contrasts sharply with his uninhibited conduct at the Merridews' party, where he abandons decorum and focuses his attention exclusively on Hester Vernon.
c25:p3: Edward, a typically reserved and proper young banker, attends a ball at the Merridews' house where he abandons his usual decorous behavior and social restraint. Captivated by the informal, permissive atmosphere of the gathering and by Hester's grown-up appearance in elegant dress, he behaves unusually boldly by monopolizing her time, dancing with her repeatedly, and withdrawing with her to the conservatory—behavior that shocks him when he later reflects upon it.
c25:p4: Edward's behavior at the Merridews' ball reveals his uncharacteristic abandonment of social propriety. After monopolizing Hester's time in the conservatory, he openly demonstrates his preference for her by refusing other dance partners and watching her intently throughout the evening, actions that alarm him upon reflection but signal his loss of emotional control to social convention.
c25:p5: Edward, having behaved uncharacteristically at the Merridews' party by abandoning his usual decorous habits and monopolizing Hester's attention, walks home in excited confusion, reflecting on his long-standing admiration for her independence and courage since childhood, now awakened by seeing her transformed into a striking young woman.
c25:p6: Edward reflects on his long-standing admiration for Hester Vernon, noting how she has transformed from a child in plain muslin at Catherine's parties into a grown woman who now attracts the attention and admiration of others at the Merridews' ball.
c25:p7: Edward reflects on his changed perception of Hester Vernon following her appearance at the Merridews' ball. Previously, he had viewed her as a dowdy child at Catherine Vernon's parties, feeling his social superiority. However, seeing her elegantly dressed with her mother's pearls at Ellen Merridew's gathering has transformed his view of her into that of a mature, striking woman worthy of serious romantic consideration.
c25:p8: Edward becomes infatuated with Hester Vernon after seeing her at the Merridews' ball, where she appears transformed from a dowdy girl into an elegant, stately young woman wearing her mother's pearls. This marks a turning point in his feelings toward her, moving beyond childhood admiration to romantic attraction intensified by her refined appearance and the permissive atmosphere of the house.
c25:p9: Edward reflects on the atmosphere at the Merridews' house during the ball, contrasting it with the restrictive social conventions he normally experiences in Redborough society. He notes the freedom and lack of parental scrutiny that characterizes their gathering, which has intoxicated him and enabled him to abandon his usual decorous behavior and pursue Hester openly.
c25:p10: Edward reflects on his uncharacteristic behavior at the Merridews' ball, where he abandoned his usual decorous restraint and devoted himself entirely to Hester Vernon's company. He acknowledges that he had unconsciously sought to lose his composure, prioritizing his own pleasure for once. The sight of Hester dressed elegantly in white with her mother's pearls intoxicated him and overcame his usual self-control, causing him to behave in ways that departed from his typical formal demeanor.
c25:p11: Edward becomes nervous the morning after the dance at the Merridews' house and deflects Catherine's questions about whom he danced with, claiming he danced little and merely enjoyed observing the party. He enthusiastically describes the conservatory's decorations to avoid directly mentioning Hester, with whom he spent much of the evening and toward whom he has developed sudden romantic interest.
c25:p12: Edward had attended a ball at the Merridews' house the previous evening, where he became infatuated with Hester Vernon, who appeared transformed by her elegant dress and pearls. The next morning at breakfast, Catherine Vernon questions him about the party. When he enthusiastically describes the conservatory with its Chinese lanterns, Catherine's dismissive response—comparing it to fairyland or the Crystal Palace—offends him deeply, as he is protective of Ellen Merridew and sensitive to any criticism of the evening that captivated him.
c25:p13: Catherine questions Edward about the expensive Merridew party at which he spent the evening with Hester, expressing concern about Algernon Merridew's financial means and suggesting Ellen's modest fortune cannot sustain such lavish entertaining.
c25:p14: Edward deflects Catherine's questioning about the expense of the Merridews' party by minimizing the cost of the Chinese lanterns, avoiding discussion of his attraction to Hester and his behavior at the event.
c25:p15: Edward has just returned from a ball at the Merridews' house where he was captivated by Hester Vernon, who has grown into an attractive young woman. At breakfast with his aunt Catherine, Edward displays uncharacteristic irritability when she questions his enthusiasm for the party and comments on its expense. Catherine now probes further into his unusual excitement about the dance, asking if he admired someone in particular.
c25:p16: Edward deflects Catherine's inquiry about whether he admired someone at the dance by suggesting they would disagree on what constitutes a "nice girl," avoiding direct mention of Hester Vernon while Catherine probes for details about his unusual excitement and interest in a particular young woman.
c25:p17: Catherine is questioning Edward about whether he admired someone at the Merridews' ball. When Edward suggests they might not agree on what constitutes "a nice girl," Catherine responds wistfully with "No?" — expressing uncertainty and hurt that Edward would not confide in her about his romantic interests, sensing a growing distance between them.
c25:p18: Catherine begins to suspect a disconnect between herself and Edward when he defensively refuses to discuss what constitutes "a nice girl." His evasiveness and changed demeanor after the Merridew ball—where he had danced extensively with Hester Vernon—prompt Catherine to question whether they truly understand each other, though she quickly dismisses this moment of doubt.
c25:p19: Catherine questions Edward about the previous evening's dance at the Merridews' house, trying to discover whom he admired. Edward has just refused to discuss what constitutes "a nice girl," prompting Catherine to ask about the belle of the party instead, hoping to extract information about his romantic interests.
c25:p20: Edward is at breakfast with his aunt Catherine Vernon. After the previous night's ball at the Merridews' house, where he became infatuated with Hester Vernon, Catherine questions him about the party. When she asks who the belle was, Edward hesitates before admitting that he was impressed by Hester, despite knowing Catherine may disapprove.
c25:p21: Edward confesses to his aunt Catherine that he admired Hester Vernon at the Merridews' ball, where she appeared as a grown woman elegantly dressed with pearls, causing him to lose his composure and behave uncharacteristically by devoting much of the evening to her attention.
c25:p22: Edward has just revealed to Catherine at breakfast that he admires Hester Vernon, who has recently come out in society and made a striking impression at a ball. Catherine learns that Hester was well-dressed with beautiful pearls, which prompts Edward's comment. Catherine receives this news with outward composure, though inwardly troubled.
c25:p23: Catherine responds to Edward's admission that he admired Hester Vernon at the Merridews' ball, masking her displeasure at learning of the girl's social success and grown beauty from Edward rather than discovering it herself.
c25:p24: At breakfast, Edward mentions to his aunt Catherine that he was impressed by Hester Vernon at the Merridews' ball—noting her beauty, elegant dress, and pearls. Catherine reacts with careful composure but feels wounded by Edward's implication that she would disapprove of his admiration for Hester, a girl whose mother (Mrs. John Vernon) lives in a house Catherine herself provided. Catherine is disturbed both by Edward's apparent success with Hester and by his assumption that she harbors negative feelings toward the girl, which damages her pride.
c25:p25: Edward tells Catherine about Hester Vernon's appearance at the Merridews' ball, mentioning Ellen's attention to her, Hester's improved looks, and notably her pearls—details that prompt Catherine's concerned reaction about Mrs. John Vernon's financial situation and possessions.
c25:p26: Catherine Vernon learns that Hester (the daughter of the widow Mrs. John Vernon) wore valuable pearls to a ball, which reveals that Mrs. John kept her settlement and jewelry despite her husband's debts. Catherine reflects bitterly on this, viewing Mrs. John as foolish for not understanding the ethical implications of retaining assets while her late husband's creditors went unpaid.
c25:p27: Edward questions Catherine about her decision to provide housing for Mrs. John Vernon, who still retains her own income from her settlement, during a breakfast conversation where Edward has just mentioned his admiration for Hester Vernon at the previous night's ball.
c25:p28: Catherine Vernon explains to Edward why she brought Mrs. John Vernon to live at the Grange despite the woman retaining part of her settlement income. Catherine describes Mrs. John as foolish for not fully surrendering her financial resources to cover her husband's debts, noting that the woman mortgaged most of her settlement to pay his creditors, leaving her with barely anything.
c25:p29: Catherine Vernon responds to Edward's question about why she brought Mrs. John Vernon to live at the Vernonry despite her possession of a personal income. Catherine explains that Mrs. John is foolish for keeping both her settlement and her pearls, which should have gone to her husband's creditors. She remarks that marrying a fool has its drawbacks, though she laughs at the irony that a woman with brains would have surrendered the settlement entirely.
c25:p30: Edward defends Mrs. John's decision to keep her settlement and pearls after her husband's financial ruin, arguing that a more intelligent woman would have surrendered them entirely to creditors.
c25:p31: Edward has just mentioned to Catherine that he admired Hester at the Merridews' ball, where she wore her mother's valuable pearls and an elegant white dress. Catherine responds with uncharacteristic sharpness to Edward's comment that a woman with brains would have given up her settlement entirely, implying the pearls may have unduly influenced his impression of Hester. She questions whether the pearls—worth considerable money—have distracted him from seeing the girl herself.
c25:p32: Edward is having breakfast with his aunt Catherine Vernon the morning after a ball at the Merridews' house. Catherine has noticed Edward's unusual excitement about the party and is questioning him about whom he admired. Edward has just admitted that he was impressed by Hester Vernon, who appeared transformed in elegant dress with her mother's pearls. Catherine expresses skepticism about the expense of the party, and Edward defensively comments on the pearls' beauty, contrasting Hester's present appearance with her previously plain, unadorned appearance at Catherine's own gatherings.
c25:p33: Edward tells Catherine that he was impressed by Hester's appearance at the Merridew ball, particularly noting her mother's pearls and elegant white dress. Catherine, initially taken aback by Edward's admiration of Hester, responds defensively by acknowledging Mrs. John's practical sense in only displaying the pearls with proper dress, while probing further details about Hester's appearance at her first ball.
c25:p34: Edward has just confessed to his aunt Catherine that he was impressed by Hester Vernon at the previous night's ball, describing her as "very handsome" in her white dress and her mother's pearls. Catherine had questioned him about his unusual excitement at the dance, and Edward deliberately reveals his admiration for Hester, sensing that this information troubles Catherine. In this moment, Edward deliberately avoids Catherine's gaze while eating breakfast calmly, fully aware that he has upset her and taking pleasure in having done so.
c25:p35: Edward, after mentioning his admiration for Hester at the previous night's ball, deflects Catherine's keen questioning about his sudden interest by asking her about John Vernon's wife (Hester's mother) and the circumstances of John Vernon's financial ruin, attempting to shift the conversation away from his own feelings toward Hester.
c25:p36: Edward has just told Catherine that he was impressed by Hester Vernon at the Merridews' ball, mentioning her beauty and her mother's pearls. Catherine, taken aback, deflects by questioning the source of Mrs. John Vernon's income and how John Vernon came to ruin. Edward presses her on whether Mrs. John's extravagance caused his downfall, prompting Catherine's response defending Mrs. John while condemning speculation as the true cause of John Vernon's financial disaster.
c25:p37: Catherine Vernon warns Edward against speculation during breakfast, contrasting it with mere extravagance as she discusses the financial ruin of John Vernon, cautioning that speculation leads only to destruction and misery.
c25:p38: Edward challenges Catherine's disapproval of financial speculation, arguing that speculation offers not only potential for great wealth but also excitement and interest as pleasures in themselves, in response to her warning about the dangers of speculation and her preference for traditional business practices.
c25:p39: Catherine Vernon warns Edward against speculation after he defends it as sometimes yielding great fortunes. She expresses her deep distrust of speculative ventures, fearing he might be tempted despite his apparent good sense. This conversation precedes Edward's later decision to secretly engage in risky financial speculation through Roland Ashton's scheme.
c25:p40: Edward responds to Catherine's warning against speculation by suggesting that some degree of risk-taking is inherent to business itself. This exchange occurs during their breakfast conversation following the Merridew party, where Catherine has been questioning Edward about his evening and expressing her concerns about financial recklessness, while Edward deflects and subtly defends the appeal of speculative ventures.
c25:p41: Catherine Vernon defends her conservative stance against speculation during a breakfast conversation with her nephew Edward, after he has attended a ball at the Merridews' house where he became infatuated with Hester Vernon. Edward has subtly challenged Catherine's objections to speculation by suggesting it has legitimate business advantages, prompting her dismissive response about her old-fashioned methods.
c25:p42: Edward, after awkwardly revealing his admiration for Hester at the Merridews' ball, deflects Catherine's questioning at breakfast by praising the party decorations. When Catherine expresses concern about the expense and hints at disapproval of Hester's newfound prominence, Edward defends himself with charming flattery about Catherine's business acumen, momentarily disarming her suspicions with his affectionate manner despite having deliberately planted seeds of doubt about Hester in her mind moments before.
c25:p43: Edward meets Hester and Emma near the Grange after returning to luncheon, but she avoids him. He then receives news at the bank that Ashton has made a profitable stock purchase on their behalf, which excites him greatly and leads him to consider a much larger speculative investment using the bank's money.
c25:p44: Edward has just had an uncomfortable breakfast with his aunt Catherine, during which he revealed his admiration for Hester Vernon and she questioned him about the Merridews' lavish party. After returning to lunch at the Grange to smooth over the tension, Edward encounters Hester and her companion Emma as he leaves to go back to the bank, an unexpected and unwelcome meeting that disturbs him.
c25:p45: Edward encounters Hester and her companion Emma while leaving the Grange. He is confused and annoyed by her reluctant behavior toward him, unable to understand why she withdraws from his greeting and avoids speaking with him, despite his recent declaration of admiration for her to Catherine at breakfast.
c25:p46: Edward encounters Hester at Catherine's Grange with Emma, but Hester avoids him and draws back from his greeting. Though Edward initially wanted to demonstrate his acquaintance with Hester to Catherine as a subtle triumph, he realizes it's better that Hester keeps her distance since he has already planted seeds of suspicion about her in Catherine's mind. Despite being piqued by Hester's coldness, Edward's attention is diverted when he arrives at the bank to receive exciting news from Roland Ashton about a profitable financial speculation opportunity.
c25:p47: Edward returns to the bank after leaving Hester and encounters Harry Vernon and Algernon Merridew who excitedly inform him that their investment broker Ashton has successfully purchased stock at a very low price with potential for substantial profits, marking the beginning of Edward's temptation toward risky financial speculation.
c25:p48: Edward arrives at the bank to find Harry Vernon and Algernon Merridew excited about a financial opportunity. Ashton has made an advantageous stock purchase at a low price with potential for significant profit. The narrator acknowledges the complexity of the financial operation while affirming that the three young men believe they understand it, comparing skillful market investment to any other purchasing transaction.
c25:p49: Algernon Merridew comments on a favorable stock purchase that Ashton has made on behalf of the young men, expressing confidence in Ashton's financial expertise and decision-making regarding an investment opportunity at a low price that promises significant returns.
c25:p50: Edward has just arrived at the bank to find Harry Vernon and Algernon Merridew in excited conversation about a profitable stock investment opportunity that Roland Ashton has arranged for them. Harry makes this remark about Ashton's eagerness to seize profitable opportunities when the market presents them.
c25:p51: Algernon Merridew is encouraging Edward and Harry Vernon to invest on a larger scale in the stock speculation opportunity that Roland Ashton has presented to them. Merridew suggests that the tight money market makes it an advantageous time to invest, implying that he and his associates have access to capital while others do not. Edward listens to this conversation with contempt, as he is already privately receiving more detailed proposals from Ashton about a much larger speculative operation using the bank's resources.
c25:p52: Harry advises caution against aggressive speculation in stocks. Edward, excited by Roland Ashton's proposition to make large profits through market operations, listens with contempt to Harry's conservative warning, dismissing it as timid. This moment reveals the tension between Harry's prudent approach and Edward's growing recklessness as he becomes seduced by the promise of financial gain.
c25:p53: Edward has just learned from Roland Ashton of a lucrative stock market opportunity. At the bank, Harry Vernon and Algernon Merridew excitedly discuss an initial profitable investment Ashton made on their behalf. Edward grows contemptuous of their limited understanding and shallow enthusiasm for the venture. He receives a far more detailed letter from Ashton proposing a much larger-scale speculation that could yield enormous profits. Tempted by this opportunity and emboldened by newfound independence, Edward dismisses Catherine's earlier warning against speculation as the fearful caution of an old woman. He reflects on his power to act boldly and alone, contemptuous of those who would hold him back.
c25:p54: Edward has just learned of a promising stock investment opportunity from his associate Roland Ashton. Despite Catherine's earlier warnings against speculation, Edward dismisses her caution as old-fashioned feminine timidity. Ashton's letter proposes a major financial operation with guaranteed success, urging Edward to keep the details confidential from his partners Harry and Algernon Merridew.
c25:p55: Edward receives an encouraging letter from Roland Ashton about a lucrative financial speculation opportunity involving stock purchases. c3:p5: **Catherine Vernon's fulfilled life as a childless woman:** The passage explains how Catherine Vernon, having never married or had children of her own, experienced the benefits of motherhood through her relationships with other people's children—particularly the well-behaved ones—while avoiding the sorrows and anxieties that come with raising one's own offspring. Her life gained purpose and occupation following a pivotal business meeting with Rule at the Grange, which transformed her existence from potential loneliness into years of meaningful work and social engagement.
c3:p6: Catherine Vernon's fulfilling life as a single woman in her old age, focused on business management and close friendships rather than marriage and children, which has protected her from the sorrows of motherhood while allowing her to enjoy the companionship and affection of many young people.
c3:p7: This chunk describes Catherine Vernon's life as an unmarried woman in her sixties, highlighting how her wealth, social position, and affectionate nature toward younger women have compensated for her lack of marriage and children. It appears within the broader passage establishing Catherine's character as a content, fulfilled spinster who has found purpose and companionship through mentoring girls and maintaining close friendships with many young households in her community.
c3:p8: The chunk appears in a passage discussing Catherine Vernon's life at age 65 as a never-married woman. The context describes how, despite being unmarried, she has enjoyed a fulfilling life filled with meaningful relationships and social connections. The chunk specifically references her having been a beloved figure to many young women and serving as an informal grandmother to numerous households. It alludes to a Biblical or poetic reference (Matthew) about childlessness, suggesting that Catherine's lack of biological children has been compensated by her deep involvement in the lives of others' children.
c3:p9: This chunk describes Catherine Vernon's physical appearance at age sixty-five, emphasizing that despite her advanced years, she retains vitality and expressiveness. It follows the narrator's reflection on whether she may have ever regretted her unmarried state, and precedes a description of her white hair and decision to retire from active business management.
c3:p10: This passage describes Catherine Vernon's physical appearance and life circumstances at age sixty, following her retirement from active work in the bank. This characterization establishes her as a benevolent, satisfied woman of means who has earned her rest, setting the stage for her role as benefactor to the poor relations and dependents she will house in the Vernonry.
c3:p11: Catherine Vernon, now sixty-five years old and retired from banking, has delegated her business responsibilities to two young male cousins, Harry and Edward Vernon, while living a peaceful life surrounded by adopted family relationships. c3:p12: Catherine Vernon, now sixty-five years old and retired from active business, has selected two young male relatives—Harry Vernon and Edward Vernon—to succeed her as partners and managers of the family bank, drawing from among the numerous descendants of the original founder John Vernon.
c3:p13: Catherine Vernon, now sixty-five years old and retired from active business, has selected two young cousins, Harry Vernon and Edward Vernon, to take over management of the Vernon bank. Both are descendants of the original founder, John Vernon, through different family lines.
c3:p14: Catherine Vernon has retired from active management of her bank at age sixty-five and has selected two young male relatives, Harry Vernon and Edward Vernon, to serve as partners and managers in her place. c3:p15: This chunk describes the living arrangements and relationships of two young men—Harry and Edward Vernon—whom Catherine Vernon has appointed as partners and managers of the family bank. c3:p16: This chunk appears in the section describing Catherine Vernon's life at age sixty-five, specifically when discussing the three young relatives—Harry Vernon, Edward Vernon, and Ellen—whom she has taken into her household and business after retiring from active work at the bank. c3:p17: This passage describes Catherine Vernon's satisfaction with the young relatives she has taken into her life, particularly Harry and Edward Vernon, whom she has made partners in the bank after retiring at sixty. c3:p18: This passage describes Catherine Vernon's relations with the young Vernons who now manage her bank business. This reflects the broader theme of Catherine's peaceful old age and her ability to avoid the worst aspects of motherhood through her detached position as elderly patroness rather than biological parent.
c3:p19: This passage describes Ellen's resistant attitude toward Catherine Vernon despite the latter's generosity and universal praise. c3:p20: Catherine Vernon's calm response to Ellen's coldness. Despite Ellen's youth and headstrong nature making her distant and unaffectionate toward her elderly cousin, Catherine Vernon accepts the situation with equanimity, believing Ellen will come to appreciate her in time.
c3:p21: Catherine Vernon has arranged for her two young cousins, Harry and Edward Vernon, to become partners and managers of the bank. Harry's sister Ellen lives with them but dislikes Catherine, though Catherine bears this coldly. Catherine has achieved the ideal of motherhood without its burdens—enjoying close relationships with good young people while avoiding the anxieties and sorrows that come with having actual children. This section marks the transition from describing Catherine's peaceful life to introducing the Heronry, the large house she converted into separate dwellings for family members and dependents.
c3:p22: Harry Vernon defends his sister Ellen's character to Catherine Vernon, who has remarked that Ellen does not like her. Harry insists that despite Ellen's foolishness and headstrong nature, she possesses a good heart, though Catherine Vernon remains unconvinced by his reassurance.
c3:p23: Catherine Vernon's calm response to Harry's defense of his sister Ellen, who has been cool and distant toward her. Despite Ellen's lack of affection, Catherine accepts the situation with equanimity, showing the tolerant wisdom of her advanced age.
c3:p24: Catherine Vernon dismisses Ellen's coldness toward her, expressing confidence that the young woman will eventually change her attitude. This exchange occurs as Catherine reflects on how her status as an unmarried benefactor allows her to escape the deepest pain of motherhood—she can enjoy the affection of grateful relatives while remaining untroubled by genuine familial discord.
c3:p25: Miss Vernon, now sixty-five years old and retired from banking, has found purpose in mentoring young relations. Two capable young men, Harry and Edward Vernon, now manage the bank she built. The chunk explains how Miss Vernon's lack of biological motherhood protects her from the deepest pain of Ellen's coldness, allowing her to focus contentedly on the devoted boys instead.
c3:p26: This chunk concludes a section describing Catherine Vernon's peaceful life at sixty-five years old, after she has retired from active business management and entrusted the bank to two young male relatives, Harry and Edward Vernon. The passage emphasizes the serenity and uneventfulness of her existence during these years.
c3:p27: This chunk introduces the Heronry, a large old house that Catherine Vernon acquires and later converts into the Vernonry—a residential compound divided into six apartments for various Vernon family relations and dependents. c3:p28: This passage describes Miss Catherine Vernon's acquisition and initial repurposing of the Heronry, a large old red-brick house located on the outskirts of Redborough. c3:p29: Catherine Vernon converts the Heronry, an old red-brick house she acquires, into six separate dwellings by dividing its many rooms into compartments, each with independent access, initiating her plan to house family members and dependents.
c3:p30: Catherine Vernon converts the old Heronry house into multiple separate dwellings by dividing it with carefully adapted doors and entrances. The townspeople of Redborough speculate about her mysterious purpose for the property, generating various rumors about what it might be used for.
c3:p31: Catherine Vernon has converted the old Heronry house into multiple dwelling compartments for family members and dependents. c3:p32: Miss Catherine Vernon has converted the old Heronry house into multiple separate dwellings for family members and dependents. This passage describes her extensive renovations to the property, including restoring the gardens and making the mysterious pool that gave the house its name safe and sanitary, as part of her larger project to create a comfortable residence for her relations.
c3:p33: This passage describes the pool at the Heronry, the old red-brick house that Catherine Vernon has converted into separate dwelling units for family members and dependents. c3:p34: This passage describes the atmospheric setting of the pool at the Heronry, one of Miss Vernon's favorite evening walks. It establishes the geographical relationship between her properties and the surrounding landscape of Redborough, emphasizing the isolated, picturesque nature of this retreat that she has developed as part of her charitable housing project.
c3:p35: This chunk appears in a passage describing the natural landscape surrounding the Heronry, the old red-brick house that Catherine Vernon has mysteriously renovated and divided into separate dwellings. c3:p36: This chunk marks the transition point in the narrative where Catherine Vernon's long-term plan for the Heronry house has been fully realized and become established in the community. c3:p37: This chunk describes the inhabitants and function of the Vernonry (formerly the Heronry), Catherine Vernon's converted house divided into six separate dwellings. It clarifies that rather than being a convent, hospital, or almshouse as townspeople had speculated, the property houses family members and dependents of the Vernon family in a residential community.
c3:p38: This passage describes the residents of the Vernonry (formerly the Heronry), the six divided dwellings that Catherine Vernon created to house poor relations and family dependents. The chunk notes that while these residents likely quarrel among themselves due to living in close quarters, they maintain propriety and discretion out of respect for Catherine Vernon's authority as their patroness.
c3:p39: This passage describes the secretive financial arrangements between Catherine Vernon and the residents of the Vernonry, the converted estate house where she housed various Vernon family members and dependents. The neighborhood's curiosity about the extent of her financial support to these relations is thwarted by the residents' deliberate discretion, protecting both their dignity and social standing.
c3:p40: This chunk describes the initial social reception and gossip in Redborough regarding the residents of the Vernonry (the converted Heronry house), explaining how Catherine Vernon's creation of six dwellings for family members and dependents was met with speculation and criticism about whether they were actually genteel almshouses for poor relations, though the residents themselves proved to be socially pretentious.
c3:p41: The revelation that Mrs. John Vernon, widow of the man who nearly destroyed the bank, will occupy the final apartment at the Vernonry—Catherine Vernon's converted estate house. This announcement shocks Redborough and introduces the return of John Vernon's widow and her daughter Hester to the town after years abroad.
c3:p42: John Vernon's financial mismanagement and wasteful spending of his wife's marriage settlement income, which contributed to the family's financial ruin and their exile abroad.
c3:p43: This passage describes how John Vernon's widow's finances were severely damaged by his debts, and introduces Hester, their young daughter, who demonstrated unusual business acumen and determination in understanding and managing the family's financial crisis. It emphasizes Hester's precocious character and her role in compelling her mother to confront the reality of their reduced circumstances following John Vernon's ruinous financial collapse and death abroad.
c3:p44: Mrs. John Vernon, widow of the man who nearly ruined the family bank, returns to Redborough to live in the Vernonry, a converted house owned by her cousin Catherine Vernon. Despite her financial downfall and exile abroad, Mrs. John's social connections—she is related to Sir John Southwood and Lady Hartingale—ensure her respectability in the town's eyes, though her decision to live so close to her former grand house and dependent on Catherine Vernon's charity remains puzzling to the townspeople.
c3:p45: Mrs. John Vernon, widow of the disgraced banker John Vernon, has decided to return to Redborough to live in one of the cottages at the Vernonry, a property owned by her wealthy cousin Catherine Vernon. Though her return surprises the townspeople, who wonder how she can bear to live near her former grand house, local society accepts her decision as her own private matter.
c3:p46: This chunk appears in the section describing Mrs. John Vernon's return to Redborough after years abroad following her husband's financial ruin of the bank. It contrasts her former state of ignorant contentment before the catastrophe with her present circumstances—now widowed, impoverished, and dependent on Catherine Vernon's charity by living in the Vernonry. The passage emphasizes the dramatic reversal of her fortune and the mystery surrounding how her husband's collapse occurred.
c3:p47: Mrs. John Vernon, the wife of the ruined banker John Vernon, reflects on her lack of understanding of the financial catastrophe that destroyed her family's fortune and forced them to leave England. Though she has learned some lessons since the crisis, she never comprehended the true causes of the collapse.
c3:p48: Mrs. John Vernon, wife of the ruined banker John Vernon, reflects on how she failed to understand the circumstances of her husband's financial collapse and their forced departure from their home, being too overwhelmed by immediate practical concerns to comprehend what had happened to them.
c3:p49: This passage describes Mrs. John Vernon's mental state during and immediately after her husband's financial ruin and their forced departure from Redborough. Overwhelmed by the practical demands of her crisis—crying, packing, and arranging travel—she lacks the emotional capacity to understand how her husband's downfall occurred. The text emphasizes her passive, unreflective nature and suggests that even after leaving England, she remains incapable of comprehending the causes of her family's catastrophe.
c3:p50: This chunk appears in a passage reflecting on Mrs. John Vernon's return to Redborough after her husband's death. She had fled the town years earlier when John Vernon nearly ruined the family bank. Now widowed and aging, she accepts Catherine Vernon's offer to live in the Heronry, a converted house divided into apartments for family members and dependents. The chunk marks the moment when Mrs. John, returning to her former home after many years abroad, begins to question what actually caused her family's downfall—a question she had been too overwhelmed to ask during the initial catastrophe.
c3:p51: Hester, a fourteen-year-old girl newly arrived at the Heronry with her widowed mother Mrs. John Vernon, takes charge of exploring their new home and understanding their family history. c3:p52: Hester, the young daughter of the disgraced John Vernon, arrives at the Heronry—a house provided by her benefactress Catherine Vernon—at age fourteen, eager to learn about her family's mysterious past and her English heritage, which she knows almost nothing about despite having lived abroad her entire life.
c3:p53: Hester, a fourteen-year-old girl newly returned to England with her widowed mother Mrs. John Vernon, reacts with excitement and curiosity to Catherine Vernon's offer of housing at the Heronry. c3:p54: Hester, a fourteen-year-old girl, persuades her reluctant mother Mrs. John Vernon to accept Catherine Vernon's offer of housing at the Heronry in Redborough, using her characteristic determination and control to overcome her mother's initial hesitation about returning to the town where their family had suffered financial ruin.
c3:p55: Hester, a fourteen-year-old girl newly arrived in England with her widowed mother Mrs. John Vernon, explores the Heronry—the old house that Catherine Vernon has offered them to live in. c3:p56: Hester and her mother Mrs. John Vernon arrive at the Vernonry, the house Catherine Vernon has offered them after John Vernon's financial ruin and death abroad. c3:p57: Mrs. John Vernon, returning to Redborough after years abroad following her husband's financial ruin, catches sight of the White House where she once lived in prosperity. Overcome with emotion at the sight of her former home, now lost to her, she laments her fall from wealth and status.
c3:p58: Hester and her mother Mrs. John Vernon have just arrived at the Vernonry, the house offered to them by their cousin Catherine Vernon after years of living abroad following Mr. John Vernon's financial ruin of the family bank. c3:p59: Mrs. John Vernon returns to Redborough after her husband's financial ruin and death abroad. Upon arriving at the Heronry, a house offered by Catherine Vernon, she becomes emotionally overwhelmed when she sees her former grand home, the White House. Her daughter Hester comforts her, and Mrs. John breaks down questioning why such misfortune befell her while Catherine Vernon remains unchanged and successful.
c3:p60: Hester attempts to understand her family's mysterious history and financial ruin by observing her mother's habitual emotional responses. Mrs. John Vernon, Hester's mother, has just returned to Redborough after years abroad, settling in the Vernonry—a house offered by their wealthy cousin Catherine Vernon. Upon seeing their former grand home, the White House, Mrs. John breaks down crying, unable to explain to her daughter why her father abandoned them. Hester, a perceptive fourteen-year-old, recognizes her mother's predictable patterns of grief and tries to piece together the family's past, though her interpretations are largely inaccurate.
c3:p61: Hester's speculation about her father John Vernon's financial ruin. After arriving at the Heronry, Hester attempts to understand why her father abandoned England and the family's former wealth. She theorizes he was the victim of a conspiracy by those around him, while remaining puzzled about Catherine Vernon's role in his downfall and subsequent reconciliation with the family.
c3:p62: Hester speculates about Catherine Vernon's motives for sheltering her family after her father John Vernon's financial ruin. c3:p63: Hester, newly arrived at the Heronry with her mother Mrs. John Vernon, tends to her mother after their emotional visit to the White House where they formerly lived. c3:p64: Hester attends to her mother Mrs. John Vernon's bedtime routine after they arrive at the Heronry, their new home provided by Miss Catherine Vernon. c3:p65: Hester tucks her mother into bed at their new home in the Vernonry, then explores the unfamiliar dark wainscoted rooms of the old house late at night, contrasting them with the bright French rooms of her childhood while pondering her father's mysterious downfall.
c3:p66: Hester explores the unfamiliar rooms of the Heronry at night, examining her new surroundings while her mother rests. c3:p67: Hester, a fourteen-year-old girl newly arrived at the Heronry with her widowed mother Mrs. John Vernon, explores the unfamiliar house at night while her mother rests. c3:p68: Hester, newly arrived at the Heronry with her mother Mrs. John Vernon, explores the old house at night. As she steps onto a verandah with her candle, she unexpectedly encounters Miss Catherine Vernon on one of her nighttime walks, marking their first meeting.
c3:p69: This passage describes Catherine Vernon's first encounter with Hester, Mrs. John Vernon's daughter, at the Vernonry (formerly the Heronry). c3:p70: Catherine Vernon encounters Hester emerging from the Heronry on a nighttime walk, and observes the girl's eager curiosity and striking appearance with some prejudice, having already formed unfavorable opinions about Mrs. John Vernon.
c30:p0: This chunk opens the final chapter of Volume II, establishing the setting for Catherine Vernon's Christmas party in Redborough—a major social event that brings together all classes of society and serves as the backdrop for key revelations about Hester's family history and her emotional awakening to the interconnected fates of those around her.
c30:p1: This passage describes the social composition of Catherine Vernon's Christmas party in Redborough, depicting the mixing of social classes at the event. The scene establishes the party's inclusive yet hierarchically-aware atmosphere, setting up tensions about social position that become central to the chapter's exploration of class and propriety.
c30:p2: At Catherine Vernon's Christmas party, the narrator describes the apparent social equality maintained by the hostess, while revealing the underlying class prejudices of the guests. c30:p3: Lady Freemantle remarks to Mrs. Merridew at Catherine Vernon's Christmas party that Catherine shows more comfort socializing with people of lower social standing (like the bank clerk's wife) than with the county gentry, implying this reflects Catherine's past involvement in business.
c30:p4: This chunk occurs during Catherine's Christmas party at Redborough. c30:p5: Catherine hosts a Christmas party in Redborough where social classes mix. Catherine, though she doesn't hear their words directly, observes their conspiratorial body language and understands their criticism through their gestures and eye movements.
c30:p6: This chunk appears in the section describing the misunderstandings and false conclusions drawn by various guests at Catherine Vernon's Christmas party. c30:p10: Mrs. John, feeling uncomfortable and out of place at Catherine Vernon's Christmas party, hesitates when Harry Vernon insists on seating her prominently among the fine people. c30:p11: Harry Vernon insists that Mrs. John (Hester's mother) sit in a prominent position among the upper-class guests at Catherine's Christmas party, despite Mrs. John's discomfort and desire to sit with people of her own social standing.
c30:p12: At Catherine Vernon's Christmas party in Redborough, Harry Vernon places Mrs. John (Hester's mother) in a prominent position among the fine ladies, despite her reluctance. The moment reflects the class tensions at the party and Mrs. John's displaced social status after her family's financial ruin.
c30:p13: At Catherine Vernon's Christmas party, Mrs. John (Hester's mother) is placed prominently among the fine ladies despite her reduced circumstances, causing her embarrassment. c30:p14: At Catherine Vernon's Christmas party in Redborough, Mrs. John (Hester's mother) and her daughter Hester are seated prominently among the great ladies by Harry Vernon, despite Mrs. John's discomfort with such a conspicuous placement. When Catherine notices their elevated seating arrangement among the elite guests, she expresses brief annoyance at what she perceives as an awkward social positioning that may cause Mrs. John embarrassment.
c30:p15: Catherine Vernon expresses frustration at Edward Vernon about Mrs. John's placement at the upper end of the drawing room during Catherine's Christmas party. Catherine believes Mrs. John, who has fallen in social status, would be more comfortable seated with people of her own class rather than among the great ladies, where her discomfort is visible to all guests.
c30:p16: At Catherine's Christmas party, Edward deflects blame for placing Mrs. John and Hester in an awkwardly prominent social position, denying involvement while secretly despising his own indifference to their discomfort.
c30:p17: Catherine is annoyed to discover that Harry Vernon has seated Mrs. John and Hester (poor relations whom Catherine has taken under her wing) in a prominent position among the fine ladies at her Christmas party, rather than among people of their own social standing where they would be more comfortable. c30:p18: Catherine comments on Harry Vernon's loyalty to family after learning that Edward did not place Mrs. John in the prominent position at the party that made her uncomfortable. Catherine attributes the positioning to Harry, praising his faithfulness to the family despite his other shortcomings.
c30:p19: At Catherine's Christmas party, Edward overhears Catherine criticize his lack of loyalty to the family, contrasting him unfavorably with his cousin Harry, who has positioned Mrs. John and Hester prominently among the elite guests. c30:p20: At Catherine Vernon's Christmas party, Mrs. John (Hester's mother) has been placed by Harry Vernon in a prominent position among the great ladies, despite her reduced circumstances. She feels out of place among the wealthy and aristocratic guests, though she would have been more comfortable with people of her current humble circumstances.
c30:p21: Mrs. John Vernon, who has fallen in social status after her husband's financial troubles, sits uncomfortably among the upper classes at Catherine Vernon's Christmas party. Placed prominently on a sofa by Harry Vernon despite her reluctance, she feels out of place among the elegant ladies. Looking around, she recalls her former position as a great lady and wonders if she once looked down on those of lower status, just as she now feels looked down upon.
c30:p22: A great lady with emeralds recognizes Mrs. John (Hester's mother) at Catherine's Christmas party as an old school friend, calling her by her childhood nickname "Bridget—Fidget," which brings joy and relief to Mrs. John after feeling out of place among the upper classes.
c30:p23: Mrs. John encounters an old school friend at Catherine's Christmas party. The woman with emeralds recognizes her and asks if she remembers "Bridget—Fidget," a school nickname. Mrs. John responds affirmatively while studying this stranger who has reconnected her with her past.
c30:p24: Mrs. John encounters an old schoolfriend at Catherine's Christmas party who recognizes her and uses her childhood school nickname "Bridget—Fidget," causing Mrs. John to experience a moment of joy and relief from her earlier embarrassment about being out of place among the social elite.
c30:p25: At Catherine Vernon's Christmas party, Mrs. John encounters an old school friend, the lady with emeralds, who recalls her by the childhood nickname "Bridget—Fidget." This recognition brings joy to Mrs. John, momentarily lifting her anxiety about being out of place among the upper-class guests. Hester, standing nearby in her dignified posture, observes her mother's conversation and is introduced to the stranger, while her mother mentions that Hester is her only child.
c30:p26: The lady with the emeralds, revealed to be Bridget Wilton, an old schoolfriend of Mrs. John, responds to Mrs. John's introduction of her daughter Hester by mentioning her own three children who are dancing at Catherine's Christmas party.
c30:p27: Hester attends Catherine's Christmas party with her mother, Mrs. John.
